introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.label: chapter:introduction
introduction.guidance:
The introduction establishes the intellectual context and stakes of your dissertation. It must:
1. Define the research problem with precision — what gap in knowledge does this address?
2. Situate your work within the existing literature (brief synthesis — the full review is later).
3. State your research questions or hypotheses explicitly.
4. Describe your theoretical framework and methodological approach.
5. Articulate the dissertation's original contribution.
6. Outline the chapter structure.
Harvard dissertations are read by a committee of experts — they expect scholarly precision
from the first paragraph. Avoid starting broad; engage the specific problem immediately.
Length: 15–30 pages typical.

literature_review.title: Literature Review
literature_review.label: chapter:literature
literature_review.guidance:
The literature review demonstrates mastery of the field and positions your contribution.
Harvard GSAS expectations:
• Organize thematically or methodologically, not as a sequential summary of papers.
• Identify schools of thought, debates, and key theoretical divides.
• Critically evaluate — what each approach does and fails to do.
• Build explicitly toward the gap your dissertation fills.
• Cover major journals and recent (last 5–10 years) scholarship; foundational works can be older.
Use the DOI importer to add papers from Crossref. Zotero integration is available for
importing directly from your library.
Length: 30–60 pages for a humanities or social science dissertation.

theoretical_framework.title: Theoretical Framework
theoretical_framework.label: chapter:theory
theoretical_framework.guidance:
Develop the theoretical lens through which you analyze your data or argument.
Explain: what theory you adopt, why it is the right tool for your research questions,
and how you operationalize key concepts.
In many disciplines this is integrated into the Literature Review or Methodology.
Activate as a separate chapter if your theoretical contribution is substantial.

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.label: chapter:methodology
methodology.guidance:
The methodology chapter must provide enough detail for replication. Include:
• Research design and paradigm (positivist, interpretivist, critical, mixed).
• Data collection: sources, selection criteria, sample size, instruments.
• Data analysis: procedures, software, analytic framework, validity checks.
• Positionality if relevant (qualitative research).
• Ethical approval: if human subjects were involved, include IRB approval information.
• Limitations of the methodology.
The committee will scrutinize this chapter for rigor — be precise about choices made.

results.title: Results / Findings
results.label: chapter:results
results.guidance:
Present findings objectively, without interpretstion.
• Organize by research question or thematic cluster.
• Quantitative: report descriptive statistics, inferential results (p-values, effect sizes,
 confidence intervals), tables and figures with clear captions.
• Qualitative: present themes with illustrative quotations; ensure anonymization.
• Every table and figure must be referenced in the text.
APA 7 citationtion format: use (Author, Year) throughout. Page numbers for direct quotes.

discussion.title: Discussion
discussion.label: chapter:discussion
discussion.guidance:
The discussion interprets findings in relation to theory and prior literature.
A strong Harvard dissertation discussion:
• Opens by restating the research question and summarizing the key finding.
• Connects each finding to the existing literature (confirming, contradicting, extending).
• Explains unexpected results with theoretical grounding.
• Discusses implications: theoretical (what this means for the field) and practical.
• Acknowledges limitations honestly — the committee will find them anyway.
• Suggests specific future directions tied to the limitations you identify.

conclusion.title: Conclusion
conclusion.label: chapter:conclusion
conclusion.guidance:
The conclusion synthesizes the dissertation's argument and contribution.
• Directly answer each research question or verify each hypothesis.
• State the original contribution clearly — what does the field now know that it did not before?
• Broader implications: how does this change practice, policy, or theory?
• Concrete, actionable future research directions.
Avoid merely summarizing chapters — the committee has read them.
Length: 10–20 pages.

references.title: References
references.guidance:
Harvard GSAS requires a complete bibliography of all cited works.
APA 7 format: hanging indent, alphabetical by first author's last name.
Generated automatically from your .bib file at compilation.
Expected volume: 100–300+ references for a PhD dissertation.
Use the DOI importer or Zotero tab to add references directly.
ProQuest tip: ensure all URLs include access dates for web sources.

appendices.title: Appendices
appendices.guidance:
Appendices contain supplementary material not central to the main argument:
• Survey instruments, interview guides, or data collection protocols.
• Extended data tables or additional statistical outputs.
• IRB approval letter and consent forms.
• Large code bases or algorithms (if not in the main text).
Label: Appendix A, Appendix B… with descriptive titles.
Cross-reference from the main text (see Appendix A).

introduction.label: chapter:introduction
introduction.guidance:
The introduction makes your dissertation's central argument and establishes
its intellectual stakes. A strong Harvard humanities introduction:
1. Opens with a specific scene, problem, or question — not a broad statement
  of field. The first paragraph should announce the argument.
2. Defines the central intervention: what does this dissertation claim
  that existing scholarship does not? Be explicit and confident.
3. Situates the work: historical period, geography, archive, corpus.
4. Engages the relevant literature (brief synthesis — full treatment in
  the following chapter or integrated per chapter).
5. Describes the theoretical or methodological approach.
6. Presents the chapter structure with a paragraph per chapter summarizing
  each chapter's argument (not just its content).
Chicago 17 Notes-Bibliography: citationtions appear as footnotes (or endnotes).
First citationtion of a work: full footnote. Subsequent: shortened form.
Use Ibid. only when the reference is immediately prior.
Length: 20–40 pages is standard for Harvard humanities dissertations.

literature_review.title: Historiography / State of the Field
literature_review.label: chapter:literature
literature_review.guidance:
In humanities dissertations this chapter is typically called "Historiography,"
"State of the Field," or "Theoretical and Methodological Foundations."
Rename the chapter title to match your discipline's conventions.
Harvard GSAS expectations:
• Organize thematically, by school of thought, or by methodology —
 never as a chronological summary of "what each scholar said."
• Identify the major interpretive debates and your position within them.
• Critically engage prior work: where it succeeds, where it falls short,
 and why this dissertation's approach is necessary.
• Introduce the theoretical frameworks you employ (e.g., subaltern studies,
 memory theory, critical race theory, new historicism) and justify their use.
• Be ruthlessly selective — cite the most significant work, not everything.
Chicago 17: cite primary sources and secondary literature in footnotes.
For archival work, introduce your primary source base here or in the next chapter.
Length: 20–50 pages depending on scope.

theoretical_framework.title: Theoretical Framework
theoretical_framework.label: chapter:theory
theoretical_framework.guidance:
For dissertations with substantial theoretical investment (e.g., critical theory,
philosophy, literary theory, postcolonial studies).
Develop your theoretical lens: what framework(s) do you employ, why are they
appropriate for your object of study, and how do you operationalize key concepts?
Acknowledge the framework's limitations and potential critiques.
In many humanities dissertations this is woven into the Introduction or the
Historiography chapter — activate as a standalone chapter only when your
theoretical contribution is itself part of the original argument.

methodology.title: Method and Sources
methodology.label: chapter:methodology
methodology.guidance:
Rename to fit your discipline: "Archival Method," "Textual Analysis,"
"Oral History Methodology," "Material Culture and Sources," etc.
This chapter must address:
• Primary source base: what archives, collections, manuscripts, or corpora
 did you consult? Where are they located? What are their limitations?
• Method of reading/interpretstion: how do you analyze your sources?
 (Close reading, discourse analysis, quantitative text analysis, oral history,
 ethnography, etc.)
• Language and translation: if sources are in multiple languages, explain
 your approach to translation and any transliteration conventions used.
• Positionality: how does your position as researcher affect interpretstion?
 Required for oral history and ethnographic work; appropriate for many
 other humanities methods.
• Ethical considerations: IRB approval if human subjects are involved;
 community consent for oral history archives.

results.title: Chapter Two
results.label: chapter:two
results.guidance:
Rename this section to your second chapter's actual title (e.g., "The Archive
of Silence: Memory and State Violence, 1936–1945").
In humanities dissertations, body chapters present the dissertation's argument
through sustained engagement with primary sources. Each chapter should:
• Open with a clear statement of the chapter's argument and its relationship
 to the dissertation's overall thesis.
• Develop a specific aspect of the larger argument through close analysis.
• Engage primary sources (archival documents, literary texts, images, oral
 testimonies) in depth — not as illustration but as evidence.
• Engage the relevant secondary literature in footnotes or in the body text.
• Close by connecting the chapter's findings to the broader argument and
 pointing forward to the next chapter.
Chicago 17 footnotes: use to cite, to add commentary that would interrupt
the main argument, or to acknowledge alternative interpretstions.
Typical chapter length: 40–70 pages.

discussion.title: Chapter Three
discussion.label: chapter:three
discussion.guidance:
Rename to your third chapter's actual title.
See guidance for Chapter Two — the same structural principles apply.
Additional considerations for middle chapters:
• Each chapter must stand alone as a coherent argument and also function
 as part of the dissertation's larger arc.
• Transitions between chapters matter: the conclusion of each chapter should
 anticipate the next.
• Avoid repeating material from earlier chapters — assume your reader has
 read them.
Activate additional chapters (Chapters Four, Five, etc.) using the Appendices
section or by duplicating this section. Dissertations in history and literature
typically have 4–6 body chapters.

conclusion.title: Conclusion
conclusion.label: chapter:conclusion
conclusion.guidance:
The conclusion advances the argument — it does not merely summarize the chapters.
A strong Harvard humanities conclusion:
• Restates the dissertation's central claim now enriched by the evidence
 presented across all chapters.
• Synthesizes the implications: what does this argument mean for the field,
 for related fields, or for broader public debates?
• Opens outward: suggests new questions, problems, or archives that this
 dissertation reveals but does not resolve.
• Briefly sketches the path to publication — committees will ask which
 chapters are being developed for journals or which press you are targeting.
Avoid restating chapter summaries — the committee has read the dissertation.
Length: 10–25 pages.

references.title: Bibliography
references.guidance:
Chicago 17 Notes-Bibliography: the bibliography lists all works cited.
Format: hanging indent, alphabetical by author's last name.
Divided into sections if appropriate:
 A. Primary Sources (by category: Archival Collections, Published Documents,
   Newspapers and Periodicals, Oral History Interviews, etc.)
 B. Secondary Sources (monographs, articles, dissertations, online resources)
Generated automatically from your .bib file at compilation.

biber/biblatex-chicago handles this automatically.
Expected volume: 150–500 references for a PhD dissertation in humanities.

appendices.guidance:

• Document transcriptions or translations (if too long for the main text).
• Statistical tables, data, or corpus lists.
• Interview transcripts or consent forms.
• Archival finding aids or provenance notes.
• Maps, genealogies, or chronologies.
Label: Appendix A, Appendix B… with descriptive titles.
Cross-reference from the main text (see Appendix A for the full list of…).

introduction.label: chapter:introduction
introduction.guidance:

2. Motivation: why does it matter? (Applications, open questions, limitations of prior art.)
3. Related work summary: brief overview — full treatment in the next chapter.
4. Thesis statement: explicit statement of the contribution.
5. Thesis organizetion: outline of chapters.

from the first paragraph — committees expect depth, not accessibility.
Length: 10–20 pages.

background.title: Background and Related Work
background.label: chapter:background
background.guidance:
Cover the technical foundations and prior art:
• Background: define key concepts, mathematical notation, models, and frameworks
 the reader needs to understand the contribution. Be precise — the committee
 will evaluate your mastery of the field.
• Related work: compare your approach to the most relevant prior work.
 Organize by approach (not by author): clustering methods, learning-based methods, etc.
• Clearly identify what prior work does NOT do, or where it fails — this is the gap.
• Every significant claim needs a citationtion [X]. Use the DOI importer for IEEE papers.
MIT CS/EE dissertations: cite arXiv, ACM DL, IEEE Xplore, NIPS proceedings.

methodology.title: Proposed Approach / Methodology
methodology.label: chapter:methodology
methodology.guidance:
Describe the technical approach in full detail:
• Problem formulation: formal definition of the problem (mathematical notation where applicable).
• System architecture or algorithm design.
• Key design decisions and their justifiestion.
• Theoretical analysis: complexity, convergence, bounds (if applicable).
• Implementation details relevant to correctness (not exhaustive code listings — those go in Appendices).
The description must be complete enough for an expert reader to reproduce the work.
MIT expects rigorous technical writing: use equations, pseudocode, diagrams as needed.

experiments.title: Experimental Evaluation
experiments.label: chapter:experiments
experiments.guidance:
Experimental rigor is critical at MIT. This chapter must:
• Describe the experimental setup fully: hardware (GPU model, CPU, memory), datasets,
 baselines, evaluation metrics, and hyperparameters.
• Present ablation studies to justify each major design decision.
• Compare against the strongest baselines — cherry-picking baselines is a serious deficiency.
• Report results with statistical significance: mean ± std, confidence intervals where applicable.
• Include failure cases and analysis — committees respect honest evaluation.
Figures: use vector graphics (PDF) for plots. Tables: use booktabs style (already included).
IEEE format: refer to figures as "Fig. X" in text.

discussion.title: Discussion
discussion.label: chapter:discussion
discussion.guidance:
Analyze what the results mean beyond the numbers:
• Why does the proposed method work? Provide intuition or theoretical support.
• Where does it fail, and why?
• Implications for the broader field or for applications.
• How does performance scale with data/compute/problem size?
In many MIT engineering dissertations, Discussion is merged with Results or Conclusion.
Activate as a separate chapter if the analysis is substantial.

conclusion.title: Conclusion and Future Work
conclusion.label: chapter:conclusion
conclusion.guidance:
Close with precision:
• Restate the thesis contributions — what the field now knows that it did not.
• Summarize the experimental evidence for each contribution.
• Limitations: be specific and honest.
• Future work: concrete next steps tied directly to your limitations and open questions.
 Avoid vague "future work includes applying this to other domains."
MIT dissertations are often the foundation for journal publications — the committee
will ask about publication plans; address this briefly here.
Length: 5–15 pages.

references.title: References
references.guidance:
IEEE numbered bibliography: entries appear in order of first citationtion.
Auto-generated from your .bib file at compilation.
MIT expects complete citationtions for all referenced work. Include:
• For journal papers: author(s), title, journal, vol., no., pp., month year, DOI.
• For conference papers: author(s), title, conference name, city, year, pp., DOI.
• For arXiv: include the arXiv ID and access date.
Use the DOI importer to get properly formatted IEEE entries from Crossref.
Typical PhD dissertation: 100–300 references.

appendices.title: Appendices
appendices.guidance:
Place technical details that would interrupt the main narrative:
• Extended proofs or derivations.
• Full algorithm listings or pseudocode.
• Additional experimental results (ablations, additional datasets).
• Dataset documentation or preprocessing pipelines.
• Code availability: if you are releasing code, include the URL or repository info.
MIT DSpace requires electronic submission — if you include large datasets,
consider supplementary materials rather than embedding in the PDF.
Label: Appendix A, B… with descriptive titles; reference from the main text.

copyright_page.guidance:
Strongly recommended. Standard format:
"Copyright © [Year] by [Full Name]. All rights reserved."
Alternatively, use a Creative Commons license for open access.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.guidance:
Stanford ETD requirements for the abstract:
• Maximum 350 words (ProQuest limit for PhD dissertations).
• Written in English (additional language versions may follow).
• Must be self-contained: no citationtions, no figures, no equations,
 no undefined acronyms.
Structure:
 1. One sentence stating the research problem.
 2. Methodology and approach (2–3 sentences).
 3. Key findings and results (2–3 sentences).
 4. Significance and contribution to the field (1–2 sentences).
The abstract is submitted separately to ProQuest Dissertations & Theses
and indexed in Stanford SearchWorks — write it as a standalone piece.

acknowledgements.title: Acknowledgements
acknowledgements.guidance:
Optional but standard. Acknowledge:
• Dissertation advisor and reading committee.
• Funding agencies (required if externally funded — include grant/contract
 numbers and award numbers, e.g., NSF Award #2012345).
• Collaborators, lab members, and institutions.
Typical funding acknowledgements:
• NSF: "This work was supported by the National Science Foundation
 under Grant No. [X]."
• DARPA: use the specific language required by the program office.
Typical length: half page to one page.

table_of_contents.title: Table of Contents
table_of_contents.guidance:
Generated automatically from your section headings.
Stanford requires a complete Table of Contents with accurate page numbers.
Include all front matter (abstract, acknowledgements), body chapters,
appendices, and bibliography.
Depth: chapters and major sections (levels 1–2 or 1–3 depending on complexity).

list_of_figures.title: List of Figures
list_of_figures.guidance:

Each entry: figure number, caption (abbreviated if long), page number.

list_of_tables.title: List of Tables
list_of_tables.guidance:

Enable this section if you have 5 or more tables.

introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.label: chapter:introduction
introduction.guidance:
The introduction must establish the problem, context, and original contribution:
1. Problem statement: define the technical or scientific challenge precisely.
2. Motivation: why does it matter? (Real-world applications, fundamental
  open questions, limitations of current state-of-the-art.)
3. Brief overview of related work — full treatment in the next chapter.
4. Dissertation statement: explicit statement of the thesis contribution
  (what was built, proved, or discovered).
5. Dissertation organizetion: one paragraph outlining each chapter.
IEEE citationtion style: numbered [1], [2], [3] in order of first appearance.
Stanford engineering programs expect technical precision from the first sentence —
committee members are domain experts who evaluate rigor, not accessibility.
Length: 10–25 pages.

background.title: Background and Related Work
background.label: chapter:background
background.guidance:
Establish the technical foundations and prior art your dissertation builds on:
• Background: define key concepts, models, mathematical notation, and frameworks.
 Be comprehensive — the committee and external reviewers assess your mastery.
• Related work: compare your approach to the most relevant prior work.
 Organize by theme or approach (not chronologically), e.g., model-based methods,
 data-driven methods, hybrid approaches.
• Identify explicitly what prior work does NOT achieve — this frames your gap.
• Every factual claim needs a citationtion [X]. Use the DOI importer for IEEE Xplore,
 ACM DL, arXiv, and NeurIPS/ICML/ICLR proceedings.
Stanford CS/EE dissertations often cite seminal papers alongside very recent work.

methodology.title: Proposed Approach
methodology.label: chapter:methodology
methodology.guidance:
The core technical contribution. Describe it with enough detail for replication:
• Problem formulation: precise mathematical or computational definition.
• System architecture or algorithm design (use block diagrams where helpful).
• Key design decisions and their justifiestion — why this approach and not others.
• Theoretical analysis: complexity, convergence, correctness proofs, or bounds
 (where applicable to the contribution type).
• Implementation notes relevant to correctness (full code listings → Appendix).
Stanford engineering reading committees expect formal rigor:
define all symbols, prove claims, and state assumptions explicitly.

experiments.title: Experimental Evaluation
experiments.label: chapter:experiments
experiments.guidance:
Stanford committees apply a high bar for experimental rigor. This chapter must:
• Describe the experimental setup completely: hardware (GPU model, CPU, memory,
 cluster configuration), datasets (with statistics), evaluation metrics,
 baselines, and all hyperparameters.
• Present ablation studies to validate each major design decision.
• Compare against the strongest baselines — committee members will ask why
 a particular baseline was omitted.
• Report results with statistical reliability: mean ± std, p-values, or
 confidence intervals where appropriate.
• Include failure analysis — honest evaluation of limitations is valued.
Figure formatting: use vector graphics (PDF/EPS). Tables: booktabs style.
IEEE format: refer to figures as "Fig. X" and tables as "Table X" in text.

discussion.title: Discussion
discussion.label: chapter:discussion
discussion.guidance:
Interpret results beyond the raw numbers:
• Why does the approach work? Provide intuition or theoretical grounding.
• Where and why does it fail?
• Scaling behavior: how does performance change with data, compute, or problem size?
• Broader implications for the field or for downstream applications.
In many Stanford engineering dissertations this chapter is merged with
Experimental Evaluation or Conclusion. Activate as a separate chapter when
the analytical depth justifies it.

conclusion.title: Conclusion and Future Work
conclusion.label: chapter:conclusion
conclusion.guidance:
Close with precision and honesty:
• Restate each thesis contribution — what the field now knows that it did not.
• Summarize the experimental evidence supporting each claim.
• Limitations: specific and honest — committees find them; address them first.
• Future work: concrete next steps directly tied to your limitations and
 open questions. Avoid generic statements like "apply this to new domains."
Stanford dissertations frequently lead to journal publications (TPAMI, JACM,
IEEE Trans., JMLR). The committee will ask about publication plans —
address this briefly here.
Length: 5–15 pages.

references.title: References
references.guidance:
IEEE numbered bibliography: entries appear in order of first citationtion.
Auto-generated from your .bib file at compilation.
Stanford requires complete citationtions for all referenced work. Include:
• Journal papers: author(s), title, journal, vol., no., pp., month year, DOI.
• Conference papers: author(s), title, conference name (abbreviated), city,
 year, pp., DOI.
• arXiv preprints: include arXiv ID (e.g., arXiv:2106.12345 [cs.LG])
 and submission date.
• Technical reports: institution, report number, year.
Use the DOI importer to get properly formatted IEEE entries from Crossref.
Typical PhD dissertation: 100–250 references.

appendices.title: Appendices
appendices.guidance:
Supplementary material that would interrupt the main narrative:
• Extended proofs, derivations, or mathematical details.
• Full algorithm listings or pseudocode that are too long for the main text.
• Additional experimental results: extra ablations, datasets, hyperparameter sweeps.
• Dataset documentation, data collection protocols, or preprocessing pipelines.
• Code availability: include repository URL (GitHub, Stanford Digital Repository).
 Stanford ScholarWorks can host large supplementary files.
Label: Appendix A, B… with descriptive titles; cross-reference from the main text
(e.g., "Details of the proof appear in Appendix A").

Structure for Social Sciences:

The abstract is the most-read part of the dissertation — it must make

introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.label: chapter:introduction
introduction.guidance:
The introduction defines the research puzzle and positions the dissertation's
contribution. At UChicago, Social Sciences committees expect precision and
intellectual ambition from the opening pages:
1. Research question or theoretical puzzle — state it explicitly in the first
  paragraph. What is unresolved in the literature that this dissertation addresses?
2. Motivation: why does it matter theoretically and empirically?
3. Core argument or hypothesis.
4. Brief overview of the theoretical framework and empirical strategy.
5. Preview of findings and their implications.
6. Chapter-by-chapter outline.
Chicago 17 Author-Date: in-text citationtions as (Author Year) or (Author Year, page).
Length: 15–30 pages.

literature_review.title: Theory and Literature
literature_review.label: chapter:literature
literature_review.guidance:
At UChicago, this chapter is typically titled "Theory and Literature,"
"Theoretical Framework," or "Situating the Argument."
Rename to match your department's conventions.
UChicago Social Sciences expectations:
• Organize by theoretical approach, mechanism, or debate — not as a
 sequential review of publications.
• Identify the central theoretical tension or unresolved empirical question.
• Position your argument within or against the dominant traditions.
• Derive testable hypotheses or analytical propositions from the theory.
• Be precise about what prior work establishes and where it fails.
Chicago Author-Date: use (Author Year) for all in-text citationtions.
For recent working papers or preprints, include access date.
Length: 20–50 pages.

theoretical_framework.title: Theoretical Framework
theoretical_framework.label: chapter:theory
theoretical_framework.guidance:
Activate as a separate chapter when your theoretical contribution is
substantial and distinct from the literature review.
Develop the causal argument, formal model, or conceptual framework that
drives your empirical analysis. State assumptions explicitly and derive
observable implications that the subsequent empirical chapters test.
Common in political economy, sociological theory, and rational choice work.

methodology.title: Research Design
methodology.label: chapter:methodology
methodology.guidance:
Rename to fit your approach: "Research Design," "Data and Methods,"
"Empirical Strategy," or "Case Selection and Method."
This chapter must establish the credibility of your causal claims. Include:
• Research design: observational, quasi-experimental, experimental, or
 interpretive. Justify why this design answers your research question.
• Case selection: logic of case choice; typicality, variation, or
 representativeness as appropriate.
• Data: sources, collection procedures, sample characteristics, and
 any collection instruments.
• Analytic method: regression, process tracing, comparetive-historical,
 discourse analysis, etc. Justify choices and acknowledge limitations.
• Identification strategy: how do you address confounding, endogeneity,
 or selection bias?
• IRB/ethical approval if human subjects research.
UChicago committees are rigorous about causal inference — be precise.

results.title: Empirical Analysis
results.label: chapter:results
results.guidance:
Present your primary empirical findings. Rename to reflect your approach
(e.g., "Case Study: Brazil, 1985–2005", "Panel Analysis of OECD Countries",
"Ethnographic Evidence from Chicago's South Side").
For quantitative dissertations:
• Report main results with statistical significance, effect sizes, and
 confidence intervals.
• Present robustness checks and sensitivity analyses.
• Include Tables and Figures with clear captions; reference each in the text.
For qualitative/interpretive dissertations:
• Present cases or themes systematically, with primary source evidence.
• Tie each piece of evidence to the analytical framework.
This section may span multiple chapters — duplicate as needed.

discussion.title: Discussion
discussion.label: chapter:discussion
discussion.guidance:
Interpret findings in relation to your theoretical framework and prior literature.
• What does this evidence mean for the theory or hypothesis?
• Which findings confirm, refute, or modify the existing literature?
• Why do unexpected results occur?
• What are the scope conditions and generalizability of your findings?
In many UChicago dissertations this is integrated into the empirical chapters
or the conclusion. Activate as a standalone chapter when the analysis is
conceptually substantial.

conclusion.title: Conclusion
conclusion.label: chapter:conclusion
conclusion.guidance:
The conclusion synthesizes contributions and advances the conversation:
• Restate the dissertation's core argument with the full weight of the
 evidence behind it.
• Summarize the key empirical contributions and their theoretical implications.
• Address scope conditions: where and when do your findings apply?
• Policy implications (where relevant to your field).
• Future research: specific questions opened by your findings that require
 different data, methods, or theoretical frameworks.
Do not merely restate chapter summaries — advance the argument.
Length: 10–25 pages.

references.title: References
references.guidance:
Chicago 17 Author-Date: alphabetical by first author's last name,
hanging indent. Auto-generated from your .bib file at compilation.
Author-Date references differ from Notes-Bibliography:
• Books: Last, First. Year. Title. Place: Publisher.
• Articles: Last, First. Year. "Title." Journal Vol (No.): pp. DOI.
• Working papers include NBER/SSRN ID and year.
biber/biblatex-chicago handles Author-Date formatting automatically.
Expected volume: 100–400 references for a Social Sciences PhD.

appendices.title: Appendices
appendices.guidance:
Supplementary material that would interrupt the main narrative:
• Formal proofs of theoretical results.
• Additional regression tables, robustness checks, or placebo tests.
• Variable definitions, data sources, and codebook.
• Survey instruments or interview protocols.
• Supplementary case evidence.
Label: Appendix A, B… with descriptive titles.
Cross-reference from the text (see Appendix A for variable definitions).

background.title: Background and Literature Review

Technical foundations and survey of prior art:

 Identify what existing methods achieve and where they fall short.
• Gap statement: what remains unsolved and why your approach addresses it.

Nature Electronics, etc.) prior to or after dissertation submission.

methodology.title: Proposed Approach
methodology.label: chapter:methodology
methodology.guidance:

• Theoretical analysis: complexity, bounds, or convergence.
• Design decisions and their justifiestion.
• Implementation details relevant to correctness.

experiments.title: Experimental Evaluation
experiments.label: chapter:experiments
experiments.guidance:
Experimental rigor is expected by TU Delft committees. Include:
• Experimental setup: hardware, datasets (with statistics), baselines,

• Ablation studies for major design decisions.
• Comparison against the strongest relevant baselines.
• Statistical reliability: mean ± std, confidence intervals, or
 significance tests across multiple runs.
• Honest failure analysis.
TU Delft values both fundamental results and practical applicability.
Include validation on real-world or industrially relevant benchmarks
where your research has practical motivation.

discussion.title: Discussion
discussion.label: chapter:discussion
discussion.guidance:
Interpret results in broader context:
• Why does the method work? Theoretical intuition.
• Where and why does it fail?
• Scalability and generalisability.
• Industrial or societal implications.
Often merged with Experimental Evaluation in TU Delft engineering theses.

conclusion.title: Conclusions and Recommendations

• Restate each contribution with supporting evidence.
• Limitations: specific and honest.
• Recommendations (aanbevelingen): concrete future research directions

• Valorisation: TU Delft encourages a brief note on the societal and

  submitted, or am submitting, for a degree or diploma or other qualification

Adapt the bracketed text per your Degree Committee's specific wording.

Cambridge Graduate Office: abstract must not exceed 300 words.
The abstract must be bound in the thesis.
Required header: university name, full name, thesis title, degree, date.
Content: summarise the problem, method, main results, and conclusions.
No citationtions, no abbreviations unless defined, no footnotes.
The abstract is separately submitted to ProQuest/EThOS for indexing —
every word counts for discoverability.

acknowledgements.title: Acknowledgements
acknowledgements.guidance:
Acknowledge your supervisor, funding bodies (mandatory if externally funded),
collaborators, and any third-party data or material providers.
If your research involved human subjects, acknowledge ethics approval here
(e.g. "This research was approved by the Cambridge Psychology Research Ethics
Committee, reference PREC/2023/xxx").

table_of_contents.title: Table of Contents

abbreviations.title: List of Abbreviations
abbreviations.guidance:
List all abbreviations and acronyms used in the thesis.

introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.label: ch:introduction
introduction.guidance:
The introduction must establish:
1. The research problem and its significance in the field.
2. The gap in existing knowledge that your thesis addresses.
3. Your research questions or hypotheses.
4. The original contribution to knowledge (Cambridge examiners will test this directly).
5. Scope and limitations.
6. Chapter outline.
Cambridge PhD examiners expect you to articulate what is NEW in your work.
Typical length: 8–15 pages (varies by discipline).
Word limit for the entire PhD thesis: 80,000 words (excluding bibliography,
appendices, tables, and figures) for most Degree Committees.
Check your specific Degree Committee's regulations — some faculties differ.

literature_review.title: Literature Review
literature_review.label: ch:literature
literature_review.guidance:
A Cambridge PhD literature review demonstrates command of the field.
Expected depth: systematic coverage of work from the last 5–10 years,
plus seminal older works.
Structure critically — do not summarise paper by paper. Instead:
• Group by theme, methodology, or chronological development.
• Critique each strand: what it shows and what it leaves unresolved.
• Build to the gap statement that motivates your research.
Recommended sources: Web of Science, Scopus, PsycINFO, JSTOR.
Use the DOI importer in TeXisStudio to cite articles correctly in APA 7.
Tip: Cambridge examiners read the literature review to assess whether you
know the field better than any single published paper in it.

theoretical_framework.title: Theoretical Framework
theoretical_framework.label: ch:theory
theoretical_framework.guidance:
Develop the conceptual or theoretical foundation of your research.
Relevant for social science, humanities, or interdisciplinary PhDs.
Distinguish clearly between theoretical framework (the lens you use)
and literature review (the empirical context).
Include: key theoretical concepts, their definitions as you use them,
and why this framework is appropriate for your research questions.

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.label: ch:methodology
methodology.guidance:
Describe your research design with sufficient detail for replication.
For empirical/quantitative research:
• Research design (experimental, survey, longitudinal, case study).
• Sample: size, selection criteria, demographics, power analysis.
• Instruments and materials: validated scales, stimuli, apparatus.
• Procedure: exact steps participants followed.
• Analysis: statistical methods, software (with version), alpha levels.
For qualitative research:
• Epistemological position and its justifiestion.
• Data collection method (interviews, observation, document analysis).
• Sampling strategy (purposive, theoretical, snowball).
• Analysis method (thematic, grounded theory, discourse analysis).
• Reflexivity and positionality statement.
• Trustworthiness measures (member checking, thick description).
Include your ethics approval reference number.

results.title: Results
results.label: ch:results
results.guidance:
Present findings without interpretstion.
For quantitative results:
• Report descriptive statistics first (M, SD, range, N).
• Report inferential tests: test statistic, df, p-value, effect size (Cohen's d, η², r).
• Use tables for complex comparisons; figures for trends and distributions.
• APA 7 format for statistics: t(48) = 3.12, p = .003, d = 0.87.
For qualitative results:
• Organise by theme, not by participant.
• Support each theme with representative quotations (with participant codes).
• Report negative cases — instances that challenged your themes.
Do not discuss implications here — save that for the Discussion chapter.

discussion.title: Discussion
discussion.label: ch:discussion
discussion.guidance:
Interpret your results in relation to your research questions and the literature.
A strong Cambridge PhD discussion:
• Addresses each research question/hypothesis directly.
• Situates findings within the broader literature — agree, disagree, extend.
• Offers a theoretical account of unexpected results.
• Discusses practical and theoretical implications.
• Acknowledges limitations honestly — examiners credit intellectual honesty.
• Discusses threats to validity and generalisability.
Avoid merely re-stating results. The discussion is where you demonstrate
your capacity for independent scholarly reasoning.

conclusion.title: Conclusion
conclusion.label: ch:conclusion
conclusion.guidance:
Synthesise the thesis rather than summarise it.
• Articulate the original contribution to knowledge — what does your thesis
 now allow the field to say that it could not say before?
• Answer your research questions directly.
• State the practical implications for policy, practice, or future research.
• Propose specific directions for future work.
• End with a closing statement that places your work in the broader context.
Cambridge examiners will read the conclusion to judge originality.
Typical length: 5–10 pages.

references.title: References
references.guidance:
Auto-generated by Biber from your .bib file in APA 7 format.
APA 7 conventions at Cambridge: use DOI when available (mandatory for recent articles).
Do not include works not cited in the text.
For a Cambridge PhD: typically 100–300+ references.

appendices.guidance:
Appendices do NOT count toward the 80,000-word limit.
Include: interview guides, survey instruments, ethics documentation,

Each appendix should be referenced in the main text.

2. Limitations of current approaches: brief critical review — what cannot
  be done today that this thesis enables?
3. Thesis statement: explicit statement of the contributions.
  Cambridge examiners assess novelty directly — state what is new clearly.
4. Dissertation organizetion: one short paragraph per chapter.
IEEE style: citationtions are numeric [1], [2], [3] in order of first appearance.
Cambridge engineering departments expect technical precision and depth from
the opening pages. The examiners are domain experts.
Length: 10–20 pages.

background.title: Background and Related Work
background.label: chapter:background
background.guidance:
Establish the technical foundations and survey prior art:
• Background: definitions, mathematical framework, models, and algorithms
 the examiner needs to evaluate your contribution.
• Related work: compare approaches by theme — not by author.
 Identify what existing methods achieve and where they fail.
• Explicitly state the gap: what remains unsolved and why your approach
 is the right response to that gap.
• Every factual claim requires a citationtion [X]. Use the DOI importer
 for IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, arXiv.
Cambridge engineering PhDs: cite published journal and conference papers
(ICASSP, NeurIPS, CVPR, ICLR, etc.) and the most relevant arXiv preprints.

methodology.title: Proposed Methodology
methodology.label: chapter:methodology
methodology.guidance:
The core technical contribution. Must be complete enough for replication:
• Problem formulation: mathematical or computational definition.
• System design or algorithm description (with diagrams where helpful).
• Theoretical analysis: complexity, convergence, correctness, or bounds.
• Key design choices with justifiestion.
• Implementation details relevant to correctness (full listings → Appendix).
Cambridge examiners apply a strict standard: every claim must be stated
as a theorem/proposition/lemma (if formal) or as an empirically testable
hypothesis (if experimental). Ambiguity in the contribution is the most
common reason for major corrections.

experiments.title: Experimental Evaluation
experiments.label: chapter:experiments
experiments.guidance:
Cambridge examiners evaluate experimental rigor closely. Required elements:
• Experimental setup: hardware (GPU model, CPU, RAM), datasets (statistics,
 splits), baselines, evaluation metrics, and all hyperparameters.
• Ablation studies justifying each major design decision.
• Comparison against the strongest baselines — committee members know the
 literature and will notice if a key baseline is absent.
• Statistical reporting: mean ± std over multiple runs, confidence intervals
 or significance tests where appropriate.
• Honest failure analysis: where and why does the method fail?
Figure formatting: vector graphics (PDF/EPS). Tables: booktabs style.
IEEE: "Fig. X" and "Table X" in the text.

discussion.title: Discussion
discussion.label: chapter:discussion
discussion.guidance:
Interpret the results beyond the numbers:
• Why does the approach work? Can you provide theoretical intuition?
• Where does it fail, and what does that reveal about the problem?
• Scalability: how does performance change with data, compute, or problem scale?
• Generalisability: which aspects transfer to related problems?
In many Cambridge engineering theses this is merged with the Experimental
Evaluation or the Conclusion. Activate standalone only when the analytical
depth warrants it.

conclusion.title: Conclusions and Future Work
conclusion.label: chapter:conclusion
conclusion.guidance:
Cambridge examiners read the conclusion carefully — it must match the claims
in the Introduction:
• Restate each contribution with the evidence from the thesis.
 Do not introduce new claims here.
• Honest limitations: be specific about what the method cannot do.
• Future work: concrete, specific directions tied to limitations and
 open questions.
• Publications arising from the thesis: list any papers published or under
 review. Cambridge examiners require this.
Length: 5–15 pages.

references.title: References
references.guidance:
IEEE numbered bibliography: entries in order of first citationtion.
Auto-generated from your .bib file at compilation.
Cambridge requires complete citationtions. Include:
• Journal papers: author(s), title, journal, vol., no., pp., year, DOI.
• Conference papers: author(s), title, proceedings (abbreviated), city,
 year, pp., DOI.
• arXiv: author(s), title, arXiv:XXXX.XXXXX [field], year.
Use the DOI importer to obtain correctly formatted IEEE entries from Crossref.
Typical Cambridge engineering PhD: 100–250 references.

appendices.title: Appendices
appendices.guidance:
Technical material that would interrupt the main narrative:
• Extended proofs or derivations.
• Full algorithm listings or pseudocode.
• Additional experimental results and ablations.
• Dataset documentation or preprocessing pipelines.
• Code availability: repository URL (GitHub, Zenodo, etc.).
 The British Library requires data availability statements.
Label: Appendix A, B… with descriptive titles; cross-reference from the text.

methodology.label: ch:methodology
methodology.guidance:
For humanities DPhil, discuss:
• Primary sources used and their nature (archival, literary, material culture).
• Methodological approach (close reading, archival analysis, comparetive, etc.).
• Languages and translation issues if applicable.
• Scope of sources and justifiestion for selection.
This chapter is mandatory for social science DPhils; optional for some humanities theses.

chapter_1.title: Chapter 1
chapter_1.label: ch:one
chapter_1.guidance:
Each body chapter should develop one main argument.
MHRA style notes:
• Footnote citationtions: Author, Title (Place: Publisher, Year), page.
• Subsequent citationtions: Author, Short Title, page.
• Ibid. for immediately preceding source.
Chapter length: typically 8,000–15,000 words depending on total thesis length.

conclusion.title: Conclusion
conclusion.label: ch:conclusion
conclusion.guidance:
Synthesise the argument developed across all chapters.
• Restate the central thesis in light of what has been demonstrated.
• Articulate the contribution to knowledge — what does your thesis now allow
 scholars to say or think differently?
• Indicate avenues for further research.
• Oxford examiners (two appointed examiners, one internal, one external) will
 probe the conclusions in the viva voce examination.
Typical length: 4,000–8,000 words.

bibliography.title: Bibliography
bibliography.guidance:
MHRA bibliography: auto-generated by Biber, formatted per MHRA 3rd edition.
Structure: Primary Sources first, then Secondary Sources (alphabetically by author).
Include all works cited in footnotes.
For archival sources, list the repository, collection, and document reference.
The bibliography does NOT count toward the 100,000-word limit.

appendices.title: Appendices
appendices.guidance:
Appendices do NOT count toward the word limit.
Include: primary source transcriptions, data tables, interview transcripts,
archival inventories, maps, genealogical tables.
Label: Appendix A, B, C with descriptive titles.
Reference each appendix from the main text.

abnt.name: ABNT
abnt.description: Mandatory standard for all academic works submitted to Brazilian universities. NBR 6023:2018 governs bibliographic references; NBR 10520:2002 governs in-text citationtions. Required at USP, UNICAMP, UFRJ, and all federal and state universities.

apa7.name: APA 7
apa7.description: The most widely used citationtion style globally. Required by most psychology, education, and social science programs. Seventh edition (2020) introduced DOI as hyperlink, up to 20 authors, and cleaner formatting rules.

chicago17_authordate.name: Chicago 17 (Author-Date)
chicago17_authordate.description: Author-Date variant of Chicago, preferred in social sciences and economics. In-text citationtions use (Author Year) format. Required at UChicago social science programs and common in economics globally.

chicago17_notes.name: Chicago 17 (Notes)
chicago17_notes.description: Notes-Bibliography system used in humanities disciplines. Citations appear as footnotes or endnotes; a full bibliography is included at the end. Preferred at Harvard, UChicago, and many UK and US humanities departments.

gb7714.name: GB/T 7714
gb7714.description: Mandatory Chinese national standard for bibliographic references in academic works. Numeric style, ordered by appearance. Required at Tsinghua, Peking University, Fudan, Zhejiang, and all Chinese universities for Chinese-language theses.

harvard.name: Harvard
harvard.description: Author-date style similar to APA, widely used in UK and Australian universities. Common in business, management, and social science programs outside the USA. No single authoritative manual — institutions often define their own variant.

ieee.name: IEEE
ieee.description: Numeric style standard for engineering, computer science, and technology disciplines. References are numbered by order of citationtion. Widely adopted at MIT, Stanford, TU Delft, TU Munich, IIT Bombay, NUS, and virtually all engineering schools globally.

mhra.name: MHRA
mhra.description: UK humanities standard similar to Chicago Notes-Bibliography. Widely required at Oxford, Cambridge, UCL, and other Russell Group universities for dissertations in history, literature, and arts.

mla9.name: MLA 9
mla9.description: Standard for language, literature, and cultural studies in North America. Uses parenthetical author-page citationtions. Ninth edition (2021) simplified formatting rules and introduced more flexible source types.

vancouver.name: Vancouver
vancouver.description: Numeric citationtion style mandatory for health sciences and medicine worldwide. References are numbered in order of appearance. Standard for most clinical and biomedical journals indexed in MEDLINE/PubMed.
